Floating-point addition is not associative because modern computers represent real numbers with finite precision. In exact arithmetic, the expressions (a + b) + c and a + (b + c) always have the same value. In floating-point arithmetic, however, each intermediate result is usually rounded to the nearest representable number according to a format such as IEEE 754 binary32 or binary64. Changing the order of addition changes the intermediate values and therefore can change where rounding occurs.

For example, suppose a is a very large positive number, b is the corresponding large negative number, and c is comparatively small. Adding a and b first may cancel exactly, leaving c. Adding b and c first may cause c to be rounded away because it is too small to affect b; adding a afterward can then produce zero. The two mathematically equivalent evaluation orders consequently give different floating-point results. Similar effects occur in long sums even when all terms have the same sign, although cancellation and mixtures of very large and very small magnitudes often make the differences more pronounced.

A matrix multiplication computes each output entry as a dot product: a sequence of products followed by a reduction that sums those products. Large matrix multiplications are divided among vector lanes, processor cores, GPU threads, and sometimes multiple machines. For performance, implementations form partial sums independently and combine them using reduction trees. A different thread count, block size, scheduling decision, hardware architecture, or library algorithm can create a different reduction tree. Because floating-point addition is not associative, these orders need not produce identical final bits, even though they implement the same mathematical formula.

Modern hardware can introduce further variation through fused multiply-add instructions, which compute a product and addition with one final rounding rather than rounding the product separately. Fused operations are generally more accurate, but mixing fused and unfused evaluation changes results. Differences in precision, compiler optimization, handling of subnormal values, and specialized low-precision matrix units can also matter.

The discrepancies are often tiny relative to the scale of the result, but they can become significant for ill-conditioned problems, sums with severe cancellation, or later computations that amplify small perturbations. Thus repeated matrix multiplications may be numerically close without being bitwise reproducible. Exact reproducibility requires controlling the reduction order and arithmetic behavior, often at some performance cost. Fixed reduction trees, higher-precision accumulation, compensated summation, and reproducible numerical libraries can reduce or eliminate order-dependent variation, while ordinary high-performance libraries usually prioritize speed over identical results across configurations.
